title: Pale Stool: What Clay-Colored, Grey or White Poop Means and Which Tests Find the Cause
summary: Pale or clay-colored stool usually means bile is not reaching the gut. Learn liver, bile duct and pancreas causes and which blood and stool tests find why.
body_markdown:
Table of contents


**Pale, clay-colored, grey or white stool usually means that too little bile is reaching your intestine. Bile from the liver gives stool its normal brown color, so stool turns pale when the liver makes less bile or when something blocks bile from flowing out** \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003129.htm) \]. The problem usually sits in the liver, the bile ducts or the pancreas, which share one drainage system \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003129.htm) \]. A short-lived cause, such as a barium x-ray test, can also turn stool white for a few days \[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003817.htm) \].


Blood tests usually show which it is. A liver panel with direct (conjugated) bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase (ALP) and GGT separates a bile flow problem from liver cell injury \[[3](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27995906/) \]\[[4](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/liver-function-tests/) \]. A blood lipase test and a stool elastase test check the pancreas \[[5](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/lipase-tests/) \]\[[6](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/stool-elastase/) \]. Pale stool that lasts several days, or comes with yellow eyes, dark urine, belly pain or fever, needs prompt attention \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003129.htm) \]\[[7](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/gallstones/symptoms-causes) \].


## Pale stool vs normal stool color


**Normal stool is brown. Stool that looks pale, clay-colored or putty-colored may be due to problems in the biliary system** \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003129.htm) \]. People also describe the same change as grey or white stool. The biliary system is the drainage system of the liver, gallbladder and pancreas \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003129.htm) \].


Two other shapes of “pale” point in different directions:


- **Pale, clay or white and otherwise formed.** This is the pattern of too little bile reaching the stool, and yellow skin and dark urine often come with it \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003129.htm) \].
- **Pale or yellowish, bulky, greasy and foul-smelling.** This is the pattern of fat in the stool, called steatorrhea. Extra fat produces pale, large-volume, foul-smelling, loose stools \[[8](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31082099/) \]. Chronic pancreatitis can cause pale or orange-colored stools along with fatty or oily stools \[[9](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000221.htm) \].


One lighter stool is not the concern. MedlinePlus advises contacting a health care provider if your stools are not the normal brown color for several days \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003129.htm) \].


## Why stool is brown: bile and bilirubin


**Stool is brown because of bile. The liver releases bile into the intestine, and bile salts and bilirubin give stool its normal color** \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003129.htm) \]\[[10](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29261920/) \].


Bilirubin is a yellowish pigment made when old red blood cells are broken down. The liver processes it so it can be removed from the body in the stool \[[11](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003479.htm) \]. Bilirubin and its breakdown products give bile and stool their color \[[10](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29261920/) \].


So stool loses its color when bile stops reaching the intestine. MedlinePlus names two ways this happens: a liver infection that reduces bile production, or a blockage in the flow of bile out of the liver \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003129.htm) \]. The bilirubin that cannot leave in bile backs up into the blood, which is why yellow skin and dark urine often appear at the same time \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003129.htm) \].


## Harmless and temporary causes of pale stool


**The clearest harmless cause is barium, the chalky contrast liquid used in some x-ray tests of the digestive tract. MedlinePlus says it is normal for stools to be white for a few days after a barium enema** \[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003817.htm) \].


Medicines are another possible cause. MedlinePlus lists some medicines among the possible causes of clay-colored stool, and a provider will ask what medicines you take \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003129.htm) \]. Do not stop a prescribed medicine on your own. Tell the prescriber about the change in stool color.


Pale stool that clears within a few days after one of these causes fits a harmless explanation. Pale stool with no clear trigger, or that lasts several days, is worth a blood test \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003129.htm) \].


## Liver causes of pale stool


**When the liver is inflamed or scarred, it can make and release less bile, and stool turns pale** \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003129.htm) \]. MedlinePlus lists viral hepatitis, alcoholic hepatitis and biliary cirrhosis among the causes of clay-colored stool \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003129.htm) \].


These liver problems usually show up on a liver panel. Hepatitis and other liver cell injury raise ALT and AST, the enzymes released from damaged liver cells \[[12](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29494096/) \]\[[3](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27995906/) \]. For the wider range of liver conditions and their symptoms, see[liver disease symptoms and blood tests](https://mitohealth.com/blog/liver-disease-symptoms-and-blood-tests) .


## Bile duct causes: gallstones, blockage and cholestasis


**A blocked bile duct is one of the main reasons for pale stool. When bile cannot drain from the liver into the intestine, the stool loses its color and bilirubin backs up into the blood** \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003129.htm) \]\[[13](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29489239/) \].


Doctors call reduced or stopped bile flow cholestasis. It can come from inside the liver or from a blockage in the bile ducts outside it \[[13](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29489239/) \]. Causes of clay-colored stool in the bile ducts include \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003129.htm) \]:


- **Gallstones** that leave the gallbladder and block a bile duct;
- **Narrowing of the bile ducts** (biliary strictures);
- **Sclerosing cholangitis** , a scarring condition of the bile ducts;
- **Cysts of the bile ducts** ;
- **Tumors** , cancerous or not, of the liver, bile ducts or pancreas.


Most gallstones cause no symptoms. Gallstones that do not block a bile duct do not cause symptoms, and a gallbladder attack usually stops once the stone moves and no longer blocks the duct \[[7](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/gallstones/symptoms-causes) \]. A blockage that lasts more than a few hours can lead to complications \[[7](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/gallstones/symptoms-causes) \].


Cholestasis also causes itching and poor absorption of fat \[[13](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29489239/) \]. That is why a bile duct problem can make stool both pale and greasy.


## Pancreas causes of pale, greasy, floating stool


**The pancreas affects stool in two ways. Pancreatitis can block bile flow and cause clay-colored stool, and a pancreas that makes too few digestive enzymes causes pale, greasy, foul-smelling stool** \[[14](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000287.htm) \]\[[9](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000221.htm) \].


- **Acute pancreatitis** can cause clay-colored stools and mild yellowing of the skin and eyes \[[14](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000287.htm) \]. Gallstones are its most common cause: a stone that travels out of the gallbladder can block the opening that drains both bile and pancreatic enzymes \[[14](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000287.htm) \].
- **Chronic pancreatitis** scars the pancreas so it can no longer make enough enzymes to digest fat. Its digestive symptoms include foul-smelling fatty or oily stools, pale or orange-colored stools, diarrhea and weight loss \[[9](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000221.htm) \]. It is most often caused by many years of alcohol use \[[9](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000221.htm) \].
- **Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency (EPI)** is the name for too little pancreatic enzyme activity to digest food. It commonly causes fatty stools, gas, weight loss and belly pain \[[15](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32310386/) \]. Its main cause in adults is chronic pancreatitis \[[6](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/stool-elastase/) \].


Fat digestion needs bile, pancreatic enzymes and a healthy small intestine, so a problem with any one of them can cause fatty stool \[[8](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31082099/) \]. Celiac disease is another cause \[[8](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31082099/) \]. Greasy stool on its own is therefore a reason to test, not proof of a pancreas problem.


Floating stool is a weaker clue. Stools that float are most often due to gas, often from a change in diet, and floating stool alone is not a sign of illness \[[16](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003128.htm) \]. Floating, greasy, foul-smelling stool, especially with weight loss, can mean severe fat malabsorption, as in chronic pancreatitis \[[16](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003128.htm) \].


## Pale stool, dark urine and yellow eyes together


**Pale stool, dark urine and yellow skin or eyes together point to bilirubin that cannot leave the body in bile. MedlinePlus notes that yellow skin often occurs with clay-colored stools and that dark urine may also occur** \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003129.htm) \].


The bilirubin that would have colored the stool stays in the blood instead. A blocked bile duct raises[direct bilirubin](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/direct-bilirubin) , the form the liver has already processed \[[3](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27995906/) \]\[[11](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003479.htm) \]. It yellows the skin and eyes once the blood level is high enough, and MedlinePlus says a level of 2.0 mg/dL can create jaundice \[[11](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003479.htm) \].


Each of these has its own page: see[yellow eyes](https://mitohealth.com/blog/yellow-eyes) ,[dark urine](https://mitohealth.com/blog/dark-urine) and[bilirubin in urine](https://mitohealth.com/blog/bilirubin-in-urine-causes-and-meaning) . Together with belly pain or fever, this combination needs prompt care (seewhen to get prompt care below).


## Which tests find the cause of pale stool


**The first tests for pale stool are blood tests of the liver, including bilirubin split into its direct and indirect parts. Lipase and a stool elastase test check the pancreas, and imaging looks for a blocked duct** \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003129.htm) \]\[[4](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/liver-function-tests/) \]\[[17](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/pancreatitis/diagnosis) \].


Test What it adds for pale stool


Liver panel (liver function tests) Measures ALT, AST, ALP, bilirubin and albumin together. Dark urine and light-colored stool are reasons to test \[[4](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/liver-function-tests/) \]


Total, direct and indirect bilirubin A raised direct (conjugated) bilirubin points to liver disease or a blocked bile duct \[[3](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27995906/) \]\[[11](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003479.htm) \]


ALP Rises with bile duct blockage, but also comes from bone \[[18](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/alkaline-phosphatase/) \]


GGT High GGT with high ALP points to the liver or bile ducts rather than bone \[[19](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/gamma-glutamyl-transferase-ggt-test/) \]


Lipase (blood) Rises when pancreas cells are damaged. A very high level is usually a sign of acute pancreatitis \[[5](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/lipase-tests/) \]


Stool (fecal pancreatic) elastase Low levels can mean the pancreas is not releasing enough digestive enzymes \[[6](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/stool-elastase/) \]


At Mito, the **[hepatic function panel](https://mitohealth.com/products/hepatic-function-panel)** covers the core liver tests in one blood draw: ALT, AST, ALP, total and direct bilirubin, albumin and total protein. The **[fractionated bilirubin test](https://mitohealth.com/products/bilirubin-fractionated-total-direct-and-indirect)** reports total, direct and indirect bilirubin together. A **[GGT test](https://mitohealth.com/products/gamma-glutamyl-transferase-ggt)** shows whether a high ALP comes from the liver. On the pancreas side, a **[lipase test](https://mitohealth.com/products/lipase)** checks for inflammation, and the **[pancreatic elastase-1 stool test](https://mitohealth.com/products/pancreatic-elastase-1)** measures enzyme output.


Blood tests point to the likely cause but rarely finish the job. Depending on the results, a clinician may order a hepatitis virus panel, an abdominal ultrasound, CT or MRI of the liver and bile ducts, or ERCP, a procedure that looks at the bile and pancreatic ducts through an endoscope \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003129.htm) \]\[[9](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000221.htm) \]. Ultrasound can find gallstones, and an endoscopic ultrasound gives pictures of the pancreas and bile ducts \[[17](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/pancreatitis/diagnosis) \].


## Reading the patterns


**The pattern across a liver panel narrows the cause of pale stool more than any single number. Providers compare all the results and look for patterns that suggest different types of liver conditions** \[[4](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/liver-function-tests/) \].


### Cholestatic pattern: direct bilirubin with ALP and GGT


- **ALP raised far more than ALT and AST** is called a cholestatic pattern: bile is not flowing normally \[[3](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27995906/) \]. Cholestasis is marked mainly by a raised ALP \[[13](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29489239/) \].
- **A raised GGT alongside it** shows the ALP is coming from the liver or bile ducts and not from bone. A high ALP with a normal GGT points to bone instead \[[19](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/gamma-glutamyl-transferase-ggt-test/) \].
- **A raised direct bilirubin** implies liver disease or a blocked bile duct in most settings \[[3](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27995906/) \]. A normal direct bilirubin is less than 0.3 mg/dL, although ranges vary slightly between labs \[[11](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003479.htm) \]. See[high direct bilirubin](https://mitohealth.com/symptom-levels/symptoms-of-high-direct-bilirubin) and[high ALP](https://mitohealth.com/symptom-levels/symptoms-of-high-alp) .


This is the pattern that fits pale stool from blocked or slowed bile flow \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003129.htm) \]\[[13](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29489239/) \]. Bilirubin can stay normal in some cases of severe cholestasis, which can show up as itching without yellowing \[[13](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29489239/) \].


### Liver cell injury: ALT and AST lead


**ALT and AST raised far more than ALP is called a hepatocellular pattern: the liver cells themselves are injured** \[[3](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27995906/) \]. It is the pattern of hepatitis, alcohol-related liver disease and medicine reactions, and the next tests usually look for viral hepatitis, fatty liver and other liver diseases \[[3](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27995906/) \].


### Bilirubin: direct vs indirect


A total bilirubin alone cannot show why it is high. The American College of Gastroenterology recommends splitting a raised total bilirubin into direct and indirect fractions \[[3](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27995906/) \]. Disorders in which the liver processes bilirubin slowly, such as Gilbert’s syndrome, raise indirect bilirubin rather than direct bilirubin \[[20](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29494090/) \]\[[11](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003479.htm) \]. For the full comparison, see[direct vs indirect bilirubin](https://mitohealth.com/compare/direct-bilirubin-vs-indirect-bilirubin) and[Gilbert’s syndrome symptoms and blood tests](https://mitohealth.com/blog/gilberts-syndrome-symptoms-and-blood-tests) .


### Pancreas: lipase and stool elastase


- **A high lipase** suggests pancreatitis or another pancreas problem. Gallbladder disease, kidney disease and intestinal problems can also raise it \[[5](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/lipase-tests/) \].
- **A stool elastase below 200 μg/g** is usually below the healthy range and may mean EPI. Above 200 μg/g makes EPI less likely without ruling it out \[[6](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/stool-elastase/) \]. The test is better at finding severe EPI than moderate EPI, and a watery sample can make the result look falsely low \[[6](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/stool-elastase/) \].


Liver test results alone usually cannot diagnose a specific disease, and abnormal results often lead to more tests \[[4](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/liver-function-tests/) \]. Normal results do not exclude every liver condition either \[[12](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29494096/) \].


## Can pale stool be harmless or reversed?


**Pale stool can be harmless when it follows a barium x-ray test, and in many other cases it can reverse once the cause is found and treated** \[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003817.htm) \]\[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003129.htm) \]. Pale stool is a sign rather than a disease, so whether it reverses depends on the cause.


- **Barium:** white stool is normal for a few days afterward \[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003817.htm) \].
- **A gallstone in the bile duct:** a gallbladder attack usually stops when the stone moves \[[7](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/gallstones/symptoms-causes) \]. A stone that stays put, or a blocked pancreatic duct, may need a procedure to remove the stone or relieve the blockage \[[14](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000287.htm) \].
- **Hepatitis and medicine reactions:** each has its own treatment, and repeat liver tests show whether it is working \[[4](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/liver-function-tests/) \].
- **Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency:** treatment usually includes pancreatic enzyme replacement taken with meals and snacks \[[6](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/stool-elastase/) \].


Some causes involve lasting damage. Chronic pancreatitis causes irreversible damage to the pancreas \[[9](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000221.htm) \].


For babies, pale or clay-colored stools can be a sign of a bile duct problem called biliary atresia, so parents should contact their child’s provider \[[21](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/001145.htm) \].


## When to get prompt care for pale stool


**See a doctor right away if pale or light-colored stool comes with belly pain lasting several hours, nausea and vomiting, fever or chills, yellow skin or eyes, or tea-colored urine** \[[7](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/gallstones/symptoms-causes) \]. These can be signs of a serious infection or inflammation of the gallbladder, liver or pancreas \[[7](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/gallstones/symptoms-causes) \].


Also seek care right away for severe or worsening belly pain, a fast heartbeat or shortness of breath, which can be signs of severe pancreatitis \[[22](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/pancreatitis/symptoms-causes) \].


Pale stool without these signs still needs a call to your provider if it lasts several days \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003129.htm) \].

## Frequently asked questions


### What causes stool to look like clay?


Stool gets its normal brown color from bile that the liver releases into the intestine. Stool turns pale, clay or putty-colored when less bile reaches it, either because a liver infection or other liver disease reduces bile production or because the flow of bile out of the liver is blocked. Gallstones, narrowed bile ducts, hepatitis, cirrhosis, some medicines and tumors of the liver, bile ducts or pancreas are among the causes MedlinePlus lists. A liver panel with direct bilirubin is the usual first blood test.


### Can pale stools be reversed?


Often, yes, because pale stool is a sign rather than a disease, and stool color returns as bile flow returns. White stool after a barium x-ray test clears within a few days. A gallbladder attack usually stops when the gallstone moves and stops blocking the bile duct, and a lasting blockage can be relieved with a procedure. Hepatitis, medicine reactions and pancreas problems each have their own treatment. Some causes, such as chronic pancreatitis or cirrhosis, involve lasting damage, so finding the cause with blood tests comes first.


### Can pale stool be harmless?


Yes, in some situations. Stool is normally white for a few days after a barium x-ray test, and some medicines can lighten stool. A single lighter stool is not the concern. MedlinePlus advises contacting a health care provider when stools are not the normal brown color for several days, and pale stool with yellow eyes or skin, dark urine, belly pain or fever needs prompt care.


### Does pancreatitis cause pale stools?


It can. MedlinePlus lists clay-colored stools among the possible symptoms of acute pancreatitis, often because a gallstone blocks the shared opening that drains bile and pancreatic enzymes. Chronic pancreatitis can cause pale or orange-colored stools and foul-smelling, fatty or oily stools, because the damaged pancreas makes too few enzymes to digest fat. A blood lipase test checks for pancreatic inflammation, and a stool elastase test checks whether the pancreas is releasing enough digestive enzymes.
